source.title: Surgical, Cheap, and Flexible: Mitigating False Refusal in Language Models via Single Vector Ablation
source.authors: Xinpeng Wang; Chengzhi Hu; Paul Röttger; Barbara Plank

record.tranche_reason: The study extracts a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal vector and directly ablates it, and also evaluates refusal-vector addition. It extends this procedure with a separate false-refusal vector and orthogonalization.
record.gate_note: The study reports direct results for ablating a true refusal vector in Table 1, and for ablation of an orthogonalized false-refusal vector in Table 2. It also describes addition results in Figure 5 and Appendix Figure 9. Results cited from other work, including SCAN comparisons, are not recorded as this study's findings.
record.test_reason: The study extracts the Arditi-style harmful-minus-harmless direction in Llama 2-7B-Chat and ablates it, removing refusal on harmful and pseudo-harmful prompts (Table 1). It then shows that a second diff-in-means direction, orthogonalized against the first, separately mediates false refusal in five chat models (Tables 1–2), which bears on V4. It also adds the true-refusal vector (Fig. 5, Fig. 9) and reports refusal and capability effects.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that ablating a false-refusal vector, orthogonalized against the true-refusal vector, reduces false refusal while keeping harmful-query refusal and general capability. Partial orthogonalization (λ) gives fine-grained calibration. Adding the true-refusal vector increases refusal but degrades general capability, so they recommend ablation over addition. They also state that the raw diff-in-means refusal direction removes refusal regardless of prompt harmfulness.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means activations and ablation/addition as in the cited refusal-vector method, but primarily extracts a pseudo-harmful-minus-harmless vector, orthogonalizes it against a true-refusal vector, and evaluates selective false-refusal mitigation.
record.method_sensitivity: The λ orthogonalization coefficient changes safe- and harmful-prompt compliance; effects on harmful prompts differ across models. Addition strength α and λ also change refusal and general-capability outcomes.
record.problems: The paper uses string matching for many refusal measurements, while noting a gap from human annotation on harmful prompts; it uses Wildguard for the main safety evaluation. It filters candidate vectors using first-token KL change and a first-token refusal score. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The direct raw true-refusal-vector ablation result is confined to Llama 2-7B-Chat. The table labels Llama 3-8B-Chat while the setup names Llama 3-8B-Inst.
record.rows_left_out: No results were omitted under the 60-row cap. Comparisons whose values are taken directly from other papers are not included.

untested.parts: Raw true-refusal-direction ablation is shown only on Llama 2-7B-Chat, with string-matching judgment. No capability results are given for that raw ablation. Addition is not tested in isolation from the false-vector ablation.
No weight edit of the general refusal direction. The weight-edited vector is the orthogonalized false-refusal vector, designed to keep harmful refusal.
Not tested. True vs false refusal vectors are not a harmfulness-judgment vs refusal-decision split.
Not tested. Vectors are extracted separately per model.
Not tested. Heavy safety tuning of Llama 2-13B is offered only as a speculative explanation.

missing.what: λ sweep of harmful and pseudo-harmful CR and MMLU across four models. Harmful CR rises faster as λ falls for Gemma, Llama 3-8B and Llama 2-7B than for Llama 2-13B, showing model-dependent overlap of the two directions.
Layer/position distribution of candidate true vs false refusal vectors. The two overlap at λ=0 and separate as λ rises (e.g. Llama 3-8B: layer 13 vs 24).
Human-evaluated XSTest-U CR 0 and XSTest-S 85.2 for Llama 2-7B after ablation (the SCAN comparator values are cited, not this study's own).

record.verdict_notes: The record misread Table 1: rows r2, r3, r4, r6 and r7 took values from the wrong line. The original model's row (2.3/14.8/13.6) was missing as baseline. Table 2 edits the orthogonalized false-refusal vector, not the general refusal direction, so those rows were moved from V2 to V4 and V2 is untested. The record's V4 'challenges' label was reversed: finding a separable second direction for false refusal supports V4, with overlap caveats. Main results use Wildguard; Table 1 and the sweeps use string matching. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The direct true-refusal-vector ablation result is reported for Llama 2-7B-Chat; no general-capability results are reported for that raw-vector ablation. Addition results are reported for Llama 2-7B-Chat and Gemma-7B-It, not as a full multi-model test of the original single-direction recipe.

The study weight-edits its orthogonalized false-refusal vector, not a general refusal vector or a named abliteration procedure. It does not test weight editing across other released models or compare edited weights with activation ablation.
No test of attacks suppressing the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
The study tests overlap and separation between extracted true- and false-refusal vectors, not affine subspaces, cones, or a dominant direction plus a quantified set of additional directions.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Different model families are tested with separately extracted vectors; transfer of one vector across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models is not tested.
The study does not vary refusal-training method or timing. Its explanation involving safety fine-tuning is a proposed explanation, not a controlled training test.

rows.subject: L LAMA 2-7B-C HAT
rows.operation_detail: Add the true refusal vector to activations while varying addition strength and false-vector orthogonalization.
rows.measure: Compliance rate; text says it is low relative to the original model
rows.note: The authors say adding the true refusal vector induces more refusal, including on pseudo-harmful prompts.
rows.check: Fig. 5 prints numbers, so the value is readable. Under simultaneous false-vector ablation, adding the refusal vector cuts OR-Bench CR from 100 (α=0) to ~3–30. JBB stays ≥ the 3.0 baseline in many cells. The addition is confounded with the ablation, so it is not a clean test of addition on the base model.

source_check.correct: Fig. 5 prints cell values (rows α, columns λ from 0 to 1). For α≥0.2, λ≥0.6, OR-Bench CR is 3.1–75.0, against 14.8 for the original model and 96.1/89.8/65.6 at α=0 with the same λ. JBB CR is 0–4, against a baseline of 3.0.
source_check.problem: The value is readable, not figure-only. The verdict fix's 'from 100 (α=0) to ~3–30' is inaccurate: at λ≥0.6, α=0 gives 65.6–96.1, and the region spans 3.1–75.0.
